nicheStories.title: Zelensky's dangerous gambit to merge the Iran and Ukraine Wars
nicheStories.description: As Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky arrives in Washington, much indicates that he is no longer merely trying to draw greater American support into its war against Russia. Increasingly, it appears to be pursuing something far more consequential: merging the Ukraine war with the U.S.-Iran conflict into a single strategic theater.The distinction matters. If the two wars become one, Ukraine ceases to be merely a recipient of American military assistance and instead becomes a direct participant in Washington's war with Tehran. By the same token, the United States would no longer simply be Ukraine's principal arms supplier. It would become an active belligerent against Russia through a conflict that stretches from the Black Sea to the Caspian.For Kyiv, this would represent the strategic breakthrough it has sought since Russia's invasion in 2022.From the outset of the war, Ukrainian leaders consistently urged NATO to move beyond supplying weapons and intelligence. Zelensky repeatedly appealed for a NATO-enforced no-fly zone, warning that anything less amounted to allowing Russia to bomb Ukrainian cities with impunity. He pressed Western governments to provide increasingly sophisticated weapons systems long before they were politically acceptable in Washington. And he argued that victory required the West to abandon what he viewed as self-imposed escalation timidity.The Biden administration sympathized with Ukraine's predicament but consistently refused to cross several red lines. President Joe Biden rejected sending American ground troops, arguing that direct combat between U.S. and Russian forces risked a wider war between nuclear powers. He repeatedly ruled out establishing a no-fly zone because enforcing one would require U.S. pilots to shoot down Russian aircraft. His administration initially declined to provide F-16 fighter jets, long-range ATACMS missiles, and other advanced systems for fear of uncontrolled escalation, only relaxing some of those restrictions gradually after lengthy internal debate.Throughout those decisions, Washington's guiding principle remained consistent: help Ukraine defend itself without allowing the United States to become a direct combatant against Russia, while also eschewing diplomacy that could have brought the fighting to an end.Today, however, the strategic landscape has changed. The Trump administration's war with Iran has produced exactly the dilemma many critics predicted. Washington possesses overwhelming military superiority, yet it has suffered a strategic defeat at the hand of Tehran. Iran has demonstrated an ability to widen the battlefield horizontally, impose costs across multiple theaters, and force the United States to defend allies and assets far from the original front lines. Iran has escalation dominance; Trump has no good military option and he lacks the patience to pursue the diplomatic ones with discipline.Trump’s vulnerability creates a historic opening for Kyiv. Instead of appearing as a country dependent on American assistance, Ukraine can now present itself as a strategic asset capable of helping Washington turn a military debacle into a splendid victory. Ukrainian drone warfare has evolved faster than almost any military innovation during the past three years. Its experience integrating inexpensive autonomous systems into conventional warfare has few equals. Just as important, Ukraine could offer something Washington currently lacks: an opportunity to expand the conflict into an entirely new geographic theater. That is, turn Iran’s horizontal escalation against it. The Caspian Sea represents such a possibility, in the Ukrainian argument. Opening pressure against Iran from the north would complicate Tehran's military planning, force it to redistribute scarce resources, and reduce its ability to dictate where the conflict is fought. From Kyiv's perspective, offering that capability transforms Ukraine from America's benefactor to its savior.But a greater strategic prize for Kyiv would be to fuse the two conflicts into one. Such a merger would fundamentally alter the political logic of both wars. American personnel, intelligence assets, logistics, and operational planning would become increasingly intertwined across the two theaters. Russian and Iranian military cooperation would likewise encourage Washington to treat them as components of a single conflict rather than separate crises.Once that threshold is crossed, the distinction between supporting Ukraine and fighting Russia becomes progressively harder to sustain.This dynamic would also appeal to Israel. First, it would give the Iran war another lease on life. Second, it would internationalize the conflict further by drawing European governments into the Iran theater through their deep commitments to Ukraine. And third, perhaps most significantly, it would transform the political narrative. Defeating Iran would no longer be presented as a necessity to defend Israel, but rather, to defend Ukraine.Given the levels of elite and public support Ukraine enjoys — after all, it was the victim of an illegal invasion — such a framing is far more politically digestible than centering the war on Israel, given Israel’s plummeting standing in the West due to its genocide in Gaza and critical role in starting the illegal war with Iran.None of this means that Ukraine’s gamble will succeed. But Trump may be susceptible to it given his self-inflicted predicament in the Strait of Hormuz. (However, judging by the decision not to hold a press conference today, this may mean Zelensky’s meeting with Trump earlier at the White House was less than successful.)Though Biden’s Ukraine policy deserves much criticism, he is resisting this type of escalation because the risk of direct confrontation between NATO and Russia could lead to a much larger and more catastrophic war. Those concerns have not disappeared simply because the White House has changed hands or because Trump has trapped himself in a foolish war. Attempts to solve one strategic problem by broadening the scope of a conflict have often made both problems harder to resolve. The greatest danger today may not be that Trump chooses to fight two wars simultaneously, but that seemingly small escalatory steps pave the way for a disaster both Biden and Trump have sought to avoid.

nicheStories.title: Zelensky's big idea for Trump: Ukraine is the Israel of Europe
nicheStories.description: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky landed in Washington with a bang Tuesday, just days after Ukraine carried out a missile strike against an Iranian cargo ship in the Caspian Sea.The attack appears to be part of Zelensky’s effort to win over President Donald Trump, who has long had a tense relationship with the Ukrainian leader. The pitch is simple: Ukraine is the kind of partner who will take action when others won’t. As George Beebe of the Quincy Institute put it, Zelensky’s goal is to “convince President Trump that Ukraine will be an Israel-type partner for the United States in Eastern Europe, where it can serve to counter Russian aggression, contain Russian expansionism, and protect Europe and NATO.” Beyond that, Kyiv is hoping to show Trump that it is “even more valuable than America’s NATO allies,” which the president has repeatedly criticized for being insufficiently supportive of his war with Iran.Zelensky’s gambit is bold, but there is evidence that his argument is gaining purchase on the right. Just last week, MAGA media figure and pro-Israel provocateur Laura Loomer suddenly reversed her years-long criticism of Ukraine, citing in particular the relationship between Russia and Iran. During a visit to the country, she met with Zelensky and pledged to make the case to Trump that he should do more to help Ukraine. “The reality is that the Iranians are using Russian weapons to kill American soldiers and to attack the United States,” Loomer told Ukrainian media. She also highlighted Zelensky’s recent claim that Russia is supplying Iran with satellite imagery that is “helping them find and kill U.S. soldiers.”Trump, for his part, appears skeptical of this intelligence connection. “We’ll find out if that’s true,” he told reporters Monday, adding that he would ask Russian President Vladimir Putin about it. Indeed, there is good reason to doubt the idea that Ukraine is bringing “critical intelligence” to the U.S. about potential Russian involvement in the Iran war, as one Fox News show claimed. “I think that's simply false,” Beebe said. “The Ukrainians do not have better technical capability than the United States itself to track Russian intelligence satellites and understand what it is they're looking at over time."In practice, these claims are part of a “campaign that is aimed largely at convincing the U.S. public and at convincing the White House that Russia is working closely with Iran to hurt the United States and to facilitate the killing of American military personnel,” he added. “The end goal here is to bring the United States much more directly into Ukraine's conflict with Russia in ways that I don't believe serve America's interests.”In the near term, Zelensky appears to at least hope that, by helping out with Iran, he can move up on the list of Trump’s priorities and get his hands on more advanced missile defense interceptors, which the U.S. has been rapidly expending in the Middle East. Another seeming goal is to get Trump to give up on peace talks with Russia and return to the Biden administration’s policy of backing Ukraine to the hilt.But the growing entanglement of these wars is also creating concerns that we are sleepwalking into a wider war that sweeps from eastern Europe down through the Middle East. For Beebe, the best way to avoid such an escalation is for U.S. officials to engage directly with their Russian counterparts. Noting that Putin has offered to help negotiate a peace deal between Iran and the U.S., Beebe said Trump should “take up the offer” and “look to find a way with Russia to contain the dangers of escalation.”In this sense, this growing crisis may create the possibility of a broader breakthrough. “That would not only put the Iran conflict on a path toward resolution, but also would build momentum toward a compromised end to the war in Ukraine,” Beebe said.

nicheStories.title: Before Lindsey there was Fritz, an anti-Iraq war, Israel skeptic
nicheStories.description: Funeral services for Sen. Lindsey Graham, who died suddenly on July 11 at the age of 71, will take place on Tuesday in Washington and Wednesday in his home state of South Carolina.Graham was known as an astute conservative politician, a military hawk, and an ardent defender of Israel, which made him a polarizing figure in today’s political climate. Along with many world leaders, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Israeli opposition leader Yair Lapid will be attending the memorial at the National Cathedral, according to reports. But before Graham there was Democratic Sen. Fritz Hollings, with whom Graham served for two years as the junior senator for South Carolina before the older man retired in January 2005 at the age of 83. Unlike Graham, who became the senate’s standard bearer for military intervention and a boundless champion for Israel, Hollings left the Senate after 38 years deeply conflicted about the war in Iraq (he voted for it in 2002 but reversed course and became a vocal critic) and of Israel, which made him a controversial (though prescient) figure. He finished out his career accused of anti-semitism — an accusation that at the time did little to temper his attitude.Without using the term “America First,” he openly wondered whether the U.S. was too subservient to Israel’s agenda and criticized by name the role of Israel’s neoconservative supporters, suggesting they pushed Washington into one of its most disastrous wars of the modern era. Hollings wrote in Charleston’s Post and Courier in May 2004:Even President Bush acknowledges that Saddam Hussein had nothing to do with 9/11... Of course there were no weapons of mass destruction. Israel’s intelligence, Mossad, knows what’s going on in Iraq. They are the best. They have to know. Israel’s survival depends on knowing. Israel long since would have taken us to the weapons of mass destruction if there were any or if they had been removed. With Iraq no threat, why invade a sovereign country?“The answer,” Hollings surmised, was ”President Bush’s policy to secure Israel.” He called out then-Deputy Secretary of Defense Paul Wolfowitz, former Assistant Secretary of Defense Richard Perle, and Fox News pundit and syndicated columnist Charles Krauthammer for advancing the idea “that the way to guarantee Israel’s security is to spread democracy in the area.” He was referring in part to the paper titled “A Clean Break: A New Strategy for Securing the Realm,” which was written for Netanyahu in 1996 by Perle (with contributions from Doug Feith, who later worked as undersecretary of defense for policy in the Bush Pentagon during the war). It advocated in part taking Saddam Hussein out of power in Iraq as a new approach to Israel’s security in the region."He [Bush] was determined to invade and democratize Iraq to secure Israel pursuant to Richard Perle's plan of 'Clean Break,'" Hollings wrote in his 2008 memoir. “When George W. Bush was elected president, proponents of ‘Clean Break’ hit pay dirt. Suddenly, those who favored striking at Iraq held seats of power.”Hollings was one of the first lawmakers to sour on the war. Barely six months after the 2003 U.S. invasion of Iraq, he was the only senator to vote against a resolution supporting the troops, calling it “political games.” Hollings criticized Bush for pushing tax cuts instead of funding the war. “If we really supported our troops, we'd pay for this war,” he said. “Instead, we're telling our troops that they not only have to fight the war, they have to come home and pay for it, too."Hollings wished that Bush had elected to stay out of Baghdad altogether, like his father. "Papa Bush said, 'Never lead American troops into an urban guerrilla warfare and bog down in a quagmire and turn the Arab world against us,'" Hollings told CBS News’ Mike Wallace on his way out of Congress in late 2004.Later he would compare Iraq to the Vietnam War. “It’s a mistake to try to build and destroy a nation at the same time,” Hollings wrote in his autobiography. He said that the U.S. was “repeating the same wrongheaded strategy in Iraq.”He consistently asserted what others did at the time: that Bush the younger was trying to accomplish what his father couldn’t or didn’t in Iraq in 1991, adding that Vice President Dick Cheney and the neoconservatives in his inner circle spurred on his decisions."I mean, (George H.W. Bush) was against going into Baghdad,” Hollings surmised. “But I think George W. wanted to say, 'I can do what Daddy can't. I'm gonna show him that he should have gone on and everything else of that kind.' And it wasn't a problem. And of course he had the cheerleaders: Pearl and Wolfowitz and Cheney and Rumsfeld and everything saying, 'Whoopie!'"After his retirement, Hollings contended that the Iraq war killed more people than the U.S. supposedly tried to liberate, creating more terrorists and helping to lionize al-Qaeda leader and 9/11 architect Osama Bin Laden in parts of the Middle East.Hollings’ controversial column suggesting the U.S. fought in Iraq for Israel’s security was published on May 10, 2004. He was inevitably, and swiftly, accused of anti-semitism. He did not back down.The Jewish Telegraphic Agency, in a May 24 article entitled, “Not So Gentle Rhetoric from the Gentleman for South Carolina,” reported that “several American Jewish organizations reacted strongly to Hollings’ column, accusing him of ‘scapegoating the Jewish community and providing ammunition for anti-Semitic attacks.’”Abe Foxman, head of the Anti-Defamation League, said Hollings’ comments that “Bush felt tax cuts would hold his crowd together and spreading democracy in the Mideast to secure Israel would take the Jewish vote from the Democrats” was particularly egregious. “Regardless of whether one feels that America’s war on Iraq was justified, the charge that it is being fought by the U.S. on behalf of Israel grossly misrepresents the legitimate U.S. interests that are involved in the debate,” he said in a letter to Hollings.Nevertheless, Hollings said “I don’t apologize for this column.”“I want them to apologize to me (for accusing me) of anti-Semitism,” he said.That the Iraq war was fought in part for Israel of course remains a source of debate, with critics of Hollings — and even critics of the war — saying that while Netanyahu may have talked up the Iraq invasion, he and his government did not play a role in the final decision to go to war. Feith even said afterwards Israel was more focused on Iran, not Iraq, at the time.Fellow Democratic senator John Kerry, who would be nominated as the Democrats’ 2004 presidential nominee just two months after the column was published, called Hollings’ comments at the time “absurd.”“Comments such as these lend credence to unacceptable and baseless antisemitic stereotypes that have no place in America or anywhere else,” Kerry said.Sen. Hollings died in 2019 and, to this writer's knowledge, never recanted any of it.There’s a case to be made that Lindsey Graham was the last of the Cold War breed. Many call him a neoconservative, too, because he was proudly loyal to the “ironclad” U.S-Israel relationship and to Israel’s security. To him, Washington’s wars in Iraq, Syria, Iran and Libya were in both American and Israeli interests. They were partners, and he was willing to sacrifice American blood and treasure for that bond.Fritz Hollings would disagree. Many of his fellow Democrats are feeling that way today, too, as evidenced in recent congressional primaries and the vote to strip military aid from Israel in the federal budget. The American people, as evidenced in recent polls, are feeling it too. South Carolinians will mourn the death of one son this week; but it is worth remembering the words of an older, and perhaps wiser, one today.
